title: Feathers in the wind
hookLine: a folk tale: gossip is like feathers from a pillow, impossible to gather back

lines: A PILLOW, A KNIFE, A WINDY HILL.
cards: A pillow, a knife, and a windy hill. That's the whole set for a story Jewish teachers tell about speech. Someone in a small town has been spreading talk about a neighbor.

The talk turns out to be cruel, and the person, sick about it, goes to the rabbi to ask how to make it right. The rabbi says: take a feather pillow up the hill, cut it open, and come back. Strange, but easy.
The person slits the pillow, watches the wind take the feathers, and comes back, ready to be forgiven. Good, says the rabbi. Now go and gather every feather.

teach.h: A FOLK TALE, NOT A TALMUD PAGE.
teach.b: Feathers in the wind. Turn the tale four ways. First, where it comes from.
You won't find it in the Torah or the Talmud.

teach.h: EASY TO SCATTER, HARD TO GATHER.
teach.b: It's a folk tale, and tellers hang it on different rabbis and different towns. It doesn't need a well-known source to land: anyone who has opened a pillow knows how feathers behave. Second, the shape of the lesson.
Scattering takes a moment. Gathering takes forever, and still fails. Words leave in a breath, land in ears you'll never meet, and get repeated in voices that aren't yours.
Third, who the story is about. Not a villain. Someone who is sorry and wants to fix it.
The tale doesn't say repentance is useless; yesterday's repair still matters.

teach.h: EVEN REAL REGRET CAN'T RECALL THEM.
teach.b: But even real regret can't recall every feather. Some of the harm is already past reaching. Fourth, so the care belongs before the words.

teach.h: DEATH AND LIFE IN THE TONGUE.
teach.b: Proverbs puts the stakes bluntly: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue."

The tale turns that line into something you can see. And today a pillow opens with one tap. A forwarded message, a screenshot, a post: each a feather with a timestamp, blowing over hills the sender will never climb.
The moment of most control is the second before speaking, while every feather is still inside.

how: Jewish teachers, parents and schools often tell the feathers tale when teaching about lashon hara, as a picture of why harmful speech can't be fully undone.

games.q: what does “feathers in the wind” mean?
o: gossip that is harmless because it's light
words that scatter and can never all come back
the soul rising lightly after a person dies

games.q: feathers in the wind — tap the pairs.
p: cut open on a windy hill
sorry, and wanting to fix it
death and life in the tongue

games.q: you've spread cruel talk about a neighbor, and you're sorry. the rabbi tells you to cut open a feather pillow on a hill. what does he ask next?
o: buy your neighbor a new pillow.
games.why: gather every feather: the impossible task shows that words, once out, can't all be brought back.

practice: Bring to mind a conversation coming up, a call, a meeting, a group chat, and one sentence already waiting on your tongue: a joke at someone's expense, a complaint about someone absent, news that isn't yours to share.
Hold it like a pillow in your hands and ask where it could blow once it's out. Decide now, while it's still sealed, whether it goes out at all; if you pray, you can ask for a guarded mouth.

wordCard.voice: Feathers in the wind. A folk tale: harmful words, like a pillow's feathers, scatter in a moment and can never all be gathered back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: you can't gather feathers. Every one is still inside until you speak. See you on the hill.
